title: Wage Determination in Perfect Markets

titles.topic: Labour Market Forces & Government Intervention (A Level)

blocks.text: Conditions for a perfectly competitive labour market

blocks.md:
- A perfectly competitive labour market requires:

  - **many buyers and sellers**: many firms hiring and many workers supplying labour, so no individual participant can influence the wage rate
  - ***homogeneous *****labour**: all workers in the occupation are assumed to have identical skills and productivity
  - **perfect information**: all workers and firms have full knowledge of wage rates and job opportunities
  - **freedom of entry and exit**: workers can move freely between occupations and firms
- In reality these conditions are never fully met

  - labour markets are inherently imperfect due to skill differences, *asymmetric information* and *geographical immobility*
  - the perfectly competitive model is therefore a theoretical benchmark rather than a description of reality

blocks.alt: Two graphs: left shows market labour supply (SL) and demand (DL) with equilibrium at W1, Q1. Right shows firm labour with SL and marginal revenue product.
blocks.caption: In the labour market for perfectly competitive firms, the wage rate is set by the industry wage rate

blocks.md:
- The equilibrium wage rate is determined where **demand for labour (D**<sub>**L**</sub>**) = supply of labour (S**<sub>**L**</sub>**)**
- At the equilibrium wage **W₁**, the quantity of labour demanded equals the quantity supplied - **Q₁** workers are employed
- As in product markets, if the wage rate is above or below W₁, market forces push it back towards equilibrium

  - excess labour supply drives wages down; excess demand drives wages up

- In a perfectly competitive labour market, the individual firm is a **wage taker**

  - it is too small to influence the market wage rate and must pay W₁
- The firm faces a **perfectly elastic supply of labour** at W₁:

  - If it offers a lower wage, it cannot recruit any workers - all will work elsewhere at W₁
  - If it offers a higher wage, it attracts more workers than it needs and pays above the market rate unnecessarily
- Because every additional worker costs the same wage rate W₁, the supply curve is also the firm's **average cost of labour (AC**<sub>**L**</sub>**)** and **marginal cost of labour (MC**<sub>**L**</sub>**)**:

  - AC<sub>L</sub> = W₁ for every worker hired
  - MC<sub>L </sub>= W₁ for every additional worker hired
  - Therefore **S**<sub>**L**</sub>** = AC**<sub>**L**</sub>** = MC**<sub>**L**</sub>** = W₁**
- The firm's demand curve for labour is its **marginal revenue product of labour (MRP**<sub>**L**</sub>**)** curve - see [marginal revenue product theory](https://www.savemyexams.com/a-level/economics/cie/23/revision-notes/government-microeconomic-intervention/labour-market-forces-and-government-intervention/marginal-revenue-product-theory/)
- The firm maximises profit by hiring labour up to the point where **MRP**<sub>**L**</sub>** = MC**<sub>**L**</sub> - i.e. where **MRP**<sub>**L**</sub> = W₁
- Equilibrium for the individual firm occurs at wage **W₁** and employment level **Q₁**

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md:
Connect wage determination to **equilibrium and disequilibrium**: excess demand pushes wages up; excess supply pushes wages down -  the same mechanism as a product market.

For higher-mark responses, note that the perfectly competitive model predicts **allocative efficiency** - workers are paid their marginal revenue product, directing labour to its highest-value use. This is the benchmark against which imperfect labour market outcomes are judged.

blocks.name: Evaluating the perfectly competitive labour market model

blocks.text: Evaluating the perfectly competitive labour market model

blocks.md:
| Strength | Limitation | |---|---| | - Provides a clear theoretical benchmark for wage determination | - Assumes homogeneous labour

- In reality workers have different skills, experience and productivity | | - Predicts that wages adjust to clear the market

- A useful starting point for analysis | - Assumes perfect information

- In reality workers and firms face significant information asymmetries | | - Explains why wage rates tend to equalise across firms in the same occupation | - Ignores *trade union* power, minimum wages and monopsony

- All of which prevent the competitive outcome | | - The model of DL = SL is directly applicable to large unskilled labour markets | - Labour is geographically immobile

- Workers cannot always move freely to where wages are highest |
